LIU enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a 24-10 overall record and a 15-3 Northeast Conference record after beating Mercyhurst 79-70 in the NEC championship game on March 10, 2026. The Sharks won the NEC regular-season title, finished 14-1 at home, and closed the pre-tournament portion of the season on a five-game winning streak. Their schedule shows the profile clearly: quality mid-major wins over James Madison (88-79 on November 15, 2025), Missouri State (75-61 on November 24, 2025), La Salle (70-60 on December 13, 2025), and two strong league wins over Central Connecticut State, including 84-78 on January 2 and 80-59 on January 31. Against high-major athletes, LIU was competitive in an 87-83 loss at Mississippi State on December 16 before getting physically overwhelmed by Illinois, 98-58, on November 22. Those game shapes matter when projecting March matchups: LIU can beat organized Division I teams with execution and toughness, but elite size and pace can still distort them. 

Offensively, Rod Strickland’s team is traditional in structure and selective in spacing. Season-long, LIU averaged 74.1 points per game, shot 48.1 percent from the field, 36.1 percent from three, and made only 6.0 threes per game, which is the key clue: this is not a bombing team; it is a paint-touch and efficiency team built around strong half-court actions, interior finishing, and veteran decision-making. The player data points to the core actions. Jamal Fuller led the team at 16.4 points per game on 52.5 percent shooting and 43.8 percent from three, Greg Gordon scored 14.1 on 56.5 percent, and Malachi Davis added 14.4 with a team-best 3.4 assists per game. That mix suggests LIU’s staple possessions are not pure spread pick-and-roll volume, but wing entry into post isolations for Fuller, slot ball screens for Davis, and middle-third touches for Gordon cutting or ducking in. The specific game evidence supports that reading. In the 88-79 win over James Madison, LIU scored 56 first-half points and shot 7-for-10 from three in the opening half, with Fuller and Davis scoring 21 each and Davis handing out eight assists. That is the look of scripted early offense: inside-out touches, drive-and-kick rhythm, and good first-side execution before the defense can load up. In the January 31 win at CCSU, Mason Porter-Brown exploded for 29 points on 10-of-11 shooting and 5-of-6 from three, a sign that LIU will run action to free a secondary forward as a pop man or weak-side spacer when opponents over-help on Fuller and Davis. In the January 2 win over CCSU, Davis scored 23, Fuller 20, and Porter-Brown 18, while Davis and Fuller each made four threes; that game showed LIU’s best version, where their primary scorers play through ball screens and post seals but punish help with catch-and-shoot perimeter looks.

Defensively, LIU is more identity-driven than on offense. The team allowed 71.1 points per game, but the better indicators are opponent 44.5 percent overall shooting and 31.9 percent from three. In conference play, the defense sharpened further: LIU scored 72.3 per game and allowed just 64.5 while opponents shot 42.4 percent overall and 30.9 percent from three. Individually, Greg Gordon led the team with 1.8 steals per game, while Shadrak Lasu anchored the back line at 1.5 blocks per game. That statistical combination matches the film-profile from the recaps: LIU pressures drivers with strong hands at the point of attack, rotates from the nail, and contests with length around the rim rather than gambling recklessly. The best documented examples are the league adjustment wins. On January 29, after losing at Le Moyne 83-77 ten days earlier, LIU answered with an 83-61 home win and held Le Moyne to just 26 second-half points. On January 31 at CCSU, the Sharks turned a one-point halftime lead into a blowout by holding the Blue Devils to 23 second-half points. In the March 7 NEC semifinal against Wagner, LIU won 64-56, with Gordon scoring 19, Fuller 17, and Lasu 13; the total itself tells the story, as LIU dragged a rivalry game into a possession-by-possession defensive contest and won with physicality, rebounding, and rim protection.

Strickland’s coaching philosophy is visible in those score patterns. LIU does not chase tempo for its own sake; it is comfortable winning at 60, 64, or 79 depending on opponent and game state. The clearest documented adjustment history comes from games where the Sharks changed the tone after halftime or after a prior meeting. Against Mercyhurst on January 8, LIU led 39-26 at halftime, then gave up the first 15 points of the second half before surviving 60-58 on Malachi Davis’s jumper with 11 seconds left. That game showed Strickland’s willingness to trust veteran half-court creators late rather than overcomplicate. Against Le Moyne, the response from an 83-77 road loss on January 19 to an 83-61 home win on January 29 showed a tangible defensive correction. Against CCSU on January 31, LIU answered an early 10-point deficit with a 15-2 second-half run and won by 21. Against Saint Francis on February 19, with at least a share of the NEC title at stake, LIU closed a seven-point deficit in the final four minutes and won 91-89. That is a strong resume of in-season adjustment: same-opponent revenge, halftime defensive tightening, and late-game reliance on veteran creators.

Clutch execution is one of LIU’s strongest selling points. The best single-possession example is January 8 against Mercyhurst: tied 58-58 with 11 seconds left, Davis hit the game-winning jumper and Gordon secured the final rebound in a 60-58 win. On February 5 against New Haven, LIU used a 9-0 run to take control, then Fuller scored the team’s final six points to finish a 60-55 win. On February 19 at Saint Francis, LIU erased a seven-point deficit in the final four minutes; Goings tied the game at 89 with two free throws after a Fuller free throw and a Saint Francis turnover, and the Sharks closed the job in a 91-89 road win. Even the March 4 NEC quarterfinal against Chicago State, a 79-75 win, featured a late offensive foul drawn by Fuller to help seal the result. This is not a fragile favorite; it is a team comfortable in ugly endings.

The key players are all proven and clearly defined. Fuller is the first name on the board: 16.4 points, 5.5 rebounds, 2.5 assists, 43.8 percent from three, and 1.1 blocks per game over 33 games. He is the matchup problem because he scores as a face-up forward, can stretch to the arc, and still rebounds like a frontcourt piece. His standout late-season moments include 26 points against Mercyhurst in the NEC title preview context cited by WTOP, 23 points in the January 31 win at CCSU, and the late scoring sequence against New Haven. Davis is the primary late-clock guard: 14.4 points, 3.4 assists, and 1.2 steals per game, plus the January 8 game-winner versus Mercyhurst and a 23-point outing in the January 2 win over CCSU. He also reached 1,000 career points in a Shark uniform on February 26 against Chicago State. Gordon is the efficiency forward/wing connector: 14.1 points on 56.5 percent shooting, 5.5 rebounds, 2.9 assists, and 1.8 steals per game. He led the March 7 Wagner semifinal with 19 points and gives LIU its best two-way steadiness. Goings supplies secondary creation and defensive activity with 10.0 points, 4.5 rebounds, 2.2 assists, and 1.4 steals per game; his free throws were central in the comeback at Saint Francis. Lasu is the rim piece: 5.2 points, 5.4 rebounds, and 1.5 blocks per game, with 13 points in the Wagner semifinal. Porter-Brown is the swing reserve/spot starter whose shot-making can change scouting priorities; his 29 points on 10-of-11 shooting and 5-of-6 from three at CCSU was one of LIU’s most explosive individual games all year.

The notable wins show a team capable of winning in multiple styles. James Madison by nine revealed offensive ceiling and early-script precision. Missouri State by 14, after LIU was down five at halftime and won the second half 40-21, revealed toughness and adjustment capacity. La Salle by 10 showed they can grind a lower-possession game. The 80-59 road blowout at CCSU revealed defensive gear-changing. The 79-70 NEC title win over Mercyhurst confirmed LIU could solve a familiar opponent after losing 91-83 at Mercyhurst on February 21. The notable losses are just as instructive. Illinois by 40 exposed size and talent-gap issues. Mississippi State by four showed LIU can hang physically but may struggle to get the final stop against power-conference shot creation. The 55-52 loss at New Haven on February 14 and the 83-77 loss at Le Moyne on January 19 showed that if LIU’s half-court offense bogs down, the margin becomes thin.

As for Strickland’s NCAA tournament history as a head coach, there is no documented NCAA tournament game coached by Rod Strickland before 2026. LIU reached the NEC semifinals in 2025 under him, but not the NCAA field. So his head-coaching NCAA tournament history entering the 2026 tournament is: zero prior appearances, zero rounds reached.

Bottom line: LIU is an old-school tournament underdog built on veteran half-court scoring, situational defense, and real late-game composure. The Sharks do not overwhelm opponents with volume threes or depth, but they do have three double-figure scorers, a proven closer in Davis, an efficient lead scorer in Fuller, and a defense that tightened to 64.5 points allowed per game in NEC play. Against a favorite, LIU’s path is clear: shorten the game, force half-court possessions, play through Fuller and Davis, and make the final four minutes uncomfortable.

matchup-analyst:
LIU enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 24-10 overall and 15-3 in NEC play, scoring 74.1 points per game and allowing 71.1 while shooting 48.1% from the field and 36.1% from three. The core identity is a physically strong, multiple-ballhandler attack built around four experienced wings/guards — Jamal Fuller (16.4 ppg, 43.8% from three), Malachi Davis (14.4 ppg, 116 assists, 97 turnovers), Greg Gordon (14.1 ppg, 56.5% FG, 5.5 rpg, 100 assists), and Jomo Goings (10.0 ppg, 37.8% from three) — plus length behind them from Shadrak Lasu (6-8, 47 blocks) and spot size from 7-1 Isaiah Miranda. Their best offense is downhill wing creation into paint touches, cuts, and kickouts rather than heavy pure-motion ball movement; the team averages only 13.6 assists per game despite 74.1 ppg, and its assist/turnover ratio is just 1.0, which suggests a lot of offense is created by individual drives, second-effort plays, and direct actions rather than constant advantage-passing. The clearest way to disrupt that style is to wall off the first drive, force LIU to play east-west, and make Davis and Fuller finish over length after multiple reversals. That worked in LIU’s 69-53 loss at Fordham on November 20, 2025, and especially in the 98-58 loss at No. 8 Illinois on November 22, when LIU’s offense bogged down against high-major size and physicality. By contrast, when LIU gets the defense tilted early, it can avalanche runs: it beat Lehigh 87-82 after leading by as many as 19 in the first half on December 6, beat Saint Francis 67-63 after erasing a 41-31 second-half deficit with a 16-5 run on January 10, and beat Chicago State 73-56 on February 26 with a 16-2 second-half burst. 

Against pressure, LIU is not a pure press-break clinic. The season turnover margin is basically even (-0.1), and the two highest-usage creators are also the biggest turnover sources: Davis has 97 turnovers, Goings 76, Fuller 69, Gordon 64. That matters because the ball does not stay with one low-mistake point guard. If you extend and make every catch a body catch, LIU can get loose with the ball. There is not enough public play-type tracking to credibly assign an exact press PPP or zone PPP for LIU from primary free sources, so the best evidence comes from game patterns: in the 83-77 loss at Le Moyne on January 19, the Sharks gave up 83 to a middle-tier NEC opponent and lost one of their few league games away from home; in the 91-83 loss at Mercyhurst on February 21, LIU’s defense got stretched into a higher-possession, less controlled game than it prefers; and in the March 4 NEC quarterfinal against Chicago State, LIU won only 79-75 at home after letting the 8-seed keep the game live deep into the second half. The actionable takeaway is that pressure is useful not because LIU is inherently bad against any press, but because their offense is creator-heavy without elite ball security. Zone is more situational: because LIU shoots 36.1% from three as a team and Fuller is at 43.8%, passive zone will lose. The right zone tactic is a match-up zone with hard nail help on Davis and loaded gaps against Gordon’s cuts/post seals, then urgent closeouts to Fuller and Goings. 

Pace-wise, LIU is most comfortable in moderate games where its physical wings can attack before the defense is fully loaded but where the game still has enough half-court possessions for their size and rim protection to matter. The schedule shows that LIU often won games in the 60s and low 70s in NEC play — 60-58 vs Mercyhurst, 67-63 vs Saint Francis, 66-59 at FDU, 66-63 at Stonehill, 60-55 vs New Haven, 61-54 vs Stonehill, 67-57 at Wagner, 64-56 vs Wagner in the NEC semifinal — which indicates they can grind. But their most explosive wins came when the game opened up enough for their scorers to string together runs: 88-79 over James Madison, 87-82 at Lehigh, 84-78 vs CCSU, 83-61 vs Le Moyne, 80-59 at CCSU, and 91-89 at Saint Francis. To force the opposite of LIU’s comfort, you have two viable routes. First, against their NEC-grind version, speed them up with misses turned into immediate advance passes and early drag screens before Lasu and Fuller load the paint. Second, against their open-floor version, flatten the game: make or miss, get back, deny early-post seals, and force LIU to score late in clock. New Haven did exactly that in a 55-52 upset on February 14. Fordham also flattened LIU in the 69-53 game. 

Positionally, LIU’s biggest advantage is across the 2/3/4 line. Davis is 6-4, Goings 6-5, Gordon 6-5 and 210, Fuller 6-5 and 215, Sheppard 6-6 and 230, Porter-Brown 6-6, and Lasu 6-8. That lets Rod Strickland play thick, interchangeable lineups that switch more actions and bully smaller mid-major backcourts. Gordon, the NEC Defensive Player of the Year, led the team in steals and rebounding among perimeter players and added 26 blocks; Fuller added 35 blocks from a wing/forward slot; Lasu had 47 blocks. The mismatch LIU creates is strength at the guard spots and shot-blocking from non-centers. The mismatch LIU can suffer is true frontcourt size. Lasu is productive but 200 pounds at 6-8. Porter-Brown is 6-6/200. Miranda is the only 7-footer, but he was not a major-minute foundational piece statistically. Against real power size, LIU got punished by Illinois (98-58) and lost at Georgia 89-74 and at Mississippi State 87-83 despite competitive scoring. A tournament opponent with a legit 6-9 or 6-10 scorer who can finish through contact can target Lasu/Porter-Brown physically, then force weakside rotations and foul trouble. 

On isolation versus team offense tendencies, the best supported inference from available primary stats is that LIU leans more toward advantage creation by individuals than pure pass-heavy collective offense. They have four double-figure scorers, but only 13.6 assists per game and just a 1.0 A/TO ratio. Davis alone used a large volume of possessions with 440 field-goal attempts, while Fuller took 343 and Gordon 377. That shot distribution, combined with modest team assist numbers, indicates LIU is not dependent on beautiful chain passing; it is dependent on Davis/Fuller/Gordon/Goings winning first actions and then finishing or making the next simple read. I cannot responsibly provide exact isolation-play percentages without a verified play-type source, but the directional evidence strongly supports LIU being more creator-led than system-led. 

Transition offense and defense also have to be inferred carefully from accessible data. LIU averages 14.8 points off turnovers and produces 7.8 steals plus 5.4 blocks per game, so its transition offense is meaningfully fed by live-ball defense. Gordon (60 steals), Goings (46), Davis (42), Fuller (33), and Porter-Brown (28) give them multiple event creators, while Lasu’s 47 blocks trigger run-outs after rim contests. The flip side is that when opponents turn LIU’s games into repeated floor-runs and force their wings to defend in space before the shot blockers are set, the Sharks become much less sturdy, as seen in losses where opponents reached the 80s: 90 by IU Indy, 94 by Winthrop, 87 by Mississippi State, 86 by FIU, 89 by Georgia, 83 by Le Moyne, and 91 by Mercyhurst. So the practical stat-based conclusion is: LIU likes transition generated from defense-to-offense, but is less comfortable defending repeated opponent transition in high-possession games. 

As for coaching adaptability, the available game evidence says yes, LIU’s staff does make in-game adjustments. The most direct example is January 10 versus Saint Francis: down 41-31 early in the second half, LIU answered with a 16-5 run, then an 11-0 run, and forced two late turnovers to close the 67-63 win. On February 26 against Chicago State, after a 32-31 halftime edge and an early second-half deficit, LIU responded with a 16-2 run to take control. On February 28 versus FDU, LIU led 31-30 at halftime after letting the early margin evaporate, then won the second half decisively enough to finish 74-60. Those are strong indicators of bench-to-locker-room recalibration within the same game. What is harder to prove is “mid-series” in the NBA sense, because college schedules offer rematches rather than playoff series. But the rematch data is encouraging: LIU lost at Le Moyne 83-77 on January 19, then beat Le Moyne 83-61 on January 29; beat Wagner 67-57 on the road February 12, then 83-65 at home February 16, then 64-56 again in the NEC semifinal March 7; lost at Mercyhurst 91-83 on February 21, then beat Mercyhurst 79-70 in the NEC title game on March 10. That is the strongest available evidence that the staff and players do absorb prior-game lessons and counterpunch effectively. 

Concrete gameplan: To beat LIU you must 1) win the physicality battle with bigger frontcourt size, not just skill; 2) build a shell around first drives by Davis and Fuller, showing crowded gaps and forcing kickouts to secondary shooters instead of straight-line paint touches; 3) selectively press after scores because LIU’s main creators all carry real turnover volume; 4) run after makes and misses to drag Lasu/Fuller/Gordon into repeated floor-sprints and neutralize LIU’s shot-blocking setup; 5) avoid lazy zone, but use a match-up zone or packed man that tags Gordon’s interior cuts and stays attached to Fuller, their most dangerous high-efficiency perimeter scorer; 6) attack their 4/5 spots with true size and force Lasu or Porter-Brown to guard through contact; 7) keep the game out of “run segment” mode, because LIU’s best wins repeatedly feature decisive bursts — 16-5 vs Saint Francis, 16-2 vs Chicago State, 14-6 close to the first half at Chicago State on January 4. If you let LIU stack stops into momentum offense, their veteran wings take over. If you force them into long, patient, half-court possessions against length and make them play over a loaded paint for 30 seconds, they are beatable.
